catalog_quote: All of the Sara Languages have three even tones: high, mid and low: tá 'to assemble (Laga)' / ɗā 'to do' (Kaba, Laga, Ngambay) / tà 'mouth' (Kaba, Laga, Ngambay). Tone-bearing phonemes are vowels and sonorant consonants when they are in final position. When a sequence of identical vowels occurs, or when a sonorant consonant closes a syllable, complex tones occur: wàä 'millet (Laga)' ... jöó 'two (Kabba, Laga, Ngambay)'. Of the nine possible combinations, Mid-Low is extremely rare, and is found in three or four morphemes. High-Low is quite rare in most native morphemes, but common in loan words and in ideophones. The High-Low tone on the final syllable of multi-syllabic foreign words often becomes Mid tone when used in a sentences. [p. 113, 'Tonal Differences'] In Laga there are a large number of cases where the Low-Mid tone found in cognates in all the other Sara Languages appear with Low-Low tone

new_statements.rule_in_words: Laka (Laga) is a register-tone language with three level tones (high, mid, low) on every vowel and on syllable-final sonorants; sequences of tones on long vowels or closed syllables give contour tones, with Mid-Low and High-Low rare in native morphemes. The source describes lexical tone only and never mentions word stress or accent; no stress rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: Tonal, not stress: High-Low on the final syllable of polysyllabic loanwords often becomes Mid in sentence context; Laga has Low-Low where other Sara languages have Low-Mid in much core vocabulary (p. 113).
new_statements.domain_note: Word/morpheme-level lexical tone in citation forms of a lexicon; the Laga lexicon is based principally on the Bemur (Bë-mür) dialect, with Mayngaw (Mày-ngàw) variants noted (p. 108). Statement is first-hand (Keegan recorded Laga speakers in N'Djaména 2011-2014) but the 'three tones' sentence is a generalisation over Kaba, Laga and Ngambay with Laga examples.
new_statements.identity_note: Keegan's lexicon uses the name Laga (the speakers' association's preferred form) for Ethnologue/Glottolog Laka (Chad) [lap], laka1254; it is based principally on the Bemur dialect with Mayngaw variants noted. Tessmann 1930's 'Lakka' is assigned by Glottolog to the same lap. Not to be confused with Lau Laka (Nigeria, Adamawa) or Laka of Cameroon/Mbum.

sources.note: Nothing on stress or accent anywhere in the volume (a full-text search for stress/accent full text: only 'unaccented e' in an English pronunciation comparison). 'Tone' section p. 12: all Sara languages incl. Laga have three level tones (H, M, L) borne by vowels and final sonorants, with complex tones on double vowels / closed syllables; Laga introduction pp. 108-117 has 'Comments on the Phonology' (pp. 109-110) and 'Tonal Differences' (p. 113: many Laga cognates carry Low-Low where other Sara languages have Low-Mid).
